rationale: A wins because it keeps the same four strong story shapes without seasoning them with facts the update did not provide. Its “Databricks discloses a $3B run rate while signaling an IPO it won't put a date on” bakes in the caveat; B's “Why would a company chasing an IPO give away its flagship AI model?” adds “chasing” and “flagship,” neither of which the facts earn. That is not a style nit. That is how a decent angle becomes a reporter's first objection.
gaps_in_A: “an enterprise that cannot send sensitive data to a third-party API” is a defensible hypothesis, not a supplied fact. The update supports data-control concern; it does not prove a blanket cannot-send constraint.

“The prevailing belief: proprietary frontier models are the core asset, and giving one away destroys value” is a useful contrarian setup, but it needs external market context or an analyst/customer source before it becomes more than a clever frame.

“For banks and hospitals” names plausible regulated verticals, but the update supplied no Databricks buyer, vertical adoption, or use case. A correctly asks for one; until then that angle is conditional.
gaps_in_B: “ARR disclosure” is not grounded. The update says annualized revenue; ARR implies recurring revenue and a SaaS metric the facts did not supply.
“flagship AI model” is invented. The update says a new foundation model, not the flagship, core asset, or most valuable IP.

“regulated industries don't want black-box AI” and “open and inspectable” add a black-box/inspectability claim that is not in the update; an open license for fine-tuning is not automatically inspectability.
“chasing an IPO” overheats “has signaled an eventual IPO without a date.” That may look small, but markets reporters notice when you smuggle timing into a caveat.
